t: LeetCode 1623 — All Valid Triplets That Can Represent a Country
o: Three school tables must be combined into every triplet (one student from each school) whose three names are pairwise distinct and whose three IDs are pairwise distinct. In Example 1, (Alice, Tom, Jerry) and (Bob, Tom, Alice) survive; (Bob, Tom, Jerry) fails because Bob and Jerry share ID 2 even though they attend different schools. The natural mechanism is a cross join followed by six inequality filters — three on names, three on IDs. Table sizes are tiny, so materializing the Cartesian product is perfectly fine; correctness hinges on remembering that BOTH the name and the ID constraints apply independently.
k: A cross join of the three tables enumerates all candidate triplets; six pairwise inequalities enforce distinctness.
Names and IDs are independent constraints — a triplet can pass one check and fail the other (Bob vs Jerry share an ID but not a name).
Output can reach Θ(|A|·|B|·|C|) rows, so no algorithm beats cubic time in the worst case; pruning only lowers constants.

a.n: Approach 1: Triple Loop with Full Validation
a.i: Nested loops over SchoolA, SchoolB and SchoolC mirror the cross join directly; each combination is checked against the three name inequalities and three ID inequalities before being emitted. The most transparent translation of the requirements into code.
s: Loop a over SchoolA, b over SchoolB, c over SchoolC.
Skip if any two of a, b, c share a student_name.
Skip if any two share a student_id.
a.t: O(|A|·|B|·|C|) — each candidate triplet validated in O(1); matches the output-size lower bound.

a.i: Validate the (A, B) pair once before entering the innermost loop; inside it, only C-vs-A and C-vs-B checks remain. Identical asymptotics, but entire C scans are skipped for bad A-B pairs — exactly what a query planner achieves by moving predicates into JOIN ON clauses instead of a trailing WHERE.
s: Loop a over SchoolA and b over SchoolB.
Discard the pair immediately on any name or ID collision between them.
For surviving pairs loop c over SchoolC, checking only collisions of c against a and against b.
a.t: O(|A|·|B|·|C|) worst case — with substantially fewer executed comparisons per triplet.

w:
## Wrap-up

Write the triple loop first, then note it translates verbatim to SQL — the canonical answer:

```sql
SELECT a.student_name AS member_A,
       b.student_name AS member_B,
       c.student_name AS member_C
FROM SchoolA a
CROSS JOIN SchoolB b
CROSS JOIN SchoolC c
WHERE a.student_name <> b.student_name
  AND a.student_name <> c.student_name
  AND b.student_name <> c.student_name
  AND a.student_id <> b.student_id
  AND a.student_id <> c.student_id
  AND b.student_id <> c.student_id;
```

**Pitfalls:** checking only names or only IDs (both rules are required — see Bob/Jerry sharing ID 2); assuming equal names imply equal IDs across schools (the schema does not guarantee it); using INNER JOIN with ON conditions incorrectly when a plain cross product plus WHERE is clearer.

**Edge cases:** empty tables yield no rows naturally; identical students appearing in different schools are handled by the pairwise filters. **Follow-ups:** scaling to millions of rows per school (semi-join pre-filtering, bloom filters, pushing predicates into join order), or generalizing to k schools with a recursive/self-joined formulation.
